# **Question 2 Deep Dive: Design a Chat Application**

A chat application (e.g., WhatsApp, Slack, Signal) enables real-time 1:1 and group messaging, online/offline status updates, typing indicators, and reliable message delivery across heterogeneous networks and device states.

## **1\. Requirements & System Constraints**

### **Functional Requirements**

> * **1:1 Messaging:** Send and receive real-time messages between two users.  
> * **Group Messaging:** Support group chats with up to ![][image1] participants.  
> * **Message Status:** Sent, Delivered, and Read receipts (ticks).  
> * **Presence & Typing Indicators:** Real-time online/offline status updates and live typing notifications.  
> * **Offline Delivery:** Queue messages sent while a user is offline and deliver them upon re-connection.  
> * **Chat History & Persistence:** Store and sync chat history across devices.

### **Non-Functional Requirements**

> * **Ultra-Low Latency:** Sub-100 ms end-to-end delivery latency for online users.  
> * **High Availability & Fault Tolerance:** Messages must not be lost once acknowledged by the server (zero data loss).  
> * **Scalability:** Support 50 million Daily Active Users (DAU) and up to ![][image2] concurrent persistent connections.  
> * **Security:** End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) support for sensitive user communications.

## **2\. Protocol Selection & Communication Models**

| Protocol | Connection Type | Direction | Pros | Cons | Best Choice For |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **HTTP Short Polling** | Short-lived | Client ![][image11] Server | Simple to implement. | Massive overhead from repeated HTTP handshake headers; high latency. | Not recommended for chat. |
| **HTTP Long Polling** | Long-lived request | Client ![][image11] Server | Works over standard HTTP; fallback for strict firewalls. | Server overhead keeping HTTP requests open; header redundancy. | Legacy fallbacks. |
| **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** | Long-lived persistent | Server ![][image11] Client | Lightweight streaming over HTTP; auto-reconnect. | Unidirectional only; client must still use separate HTTP POST for sending. | Server alerts, news feeds. |
| **WebSockets** | Long-lived full-duplex TCP | Bi-directional | Sub-10 ms latency over single connection; minimal overhead frames (![][image12]). | Connection state management on servers; stateful routing required. | **Core Chat Engine** |

### **Why WebSockets?**

Once established via an HTTP Upgrade handshake (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols), a persistent full-duplex TCP connection remains open between client and gateway. Both parties can stream binary or text frames instantly without repeating HTTP headers.

### **Component Responsibilities**

> 1. **WebSocket Gateways:** Maintain stateful persistent TCP connections with online users. Convert incoming WebSocket frames into internal domain events.  
> 2. **User Session Store (Redis):** Maps user\_id ![][image11] gateway\_node\_id & socket\_id.  
> 3. **Message Service:** Coordinates message validation, sequence ordering, persistence, and routing.  
> 4. **Presence & Typing Service:** Tracks heartbeat states and handles high-frequency typing events using ephemeral caching.  
> 5. **Push Notification Service (APNs/FCM):** Delivers push notifications when a user is disconnected or running in background mode.

## **4\. Message Flow Mechanics**

### **1:1 Online Message Flow**

Sender (User A)       WS Gateway 1     Message Service     User Session Store    WS Gateway 2      Receiver (User B)  
     |                     |                 |                     |                  |                    |  
     |--- Send Message \---\>|                 |                     |                  |                    |  
     |    (temp\_id: 101\)   |--- Publish \----\>|                     |                  |                    |  
     |                     |                 |--- Query Gateway \--\>|                  |                    |  
     |                     |                 |    for User B       |                  |                    |  
     |                     |                 |\<-- Returns GW 2 \----|                  |                    |  
     |                     |                 |                                        |                    |  
     |                     |                 |--- Route Message \---------------------\>|                    |  
     |                     |                 |    (msg\_id: 999\)                       |--- Push Message \--\>|  
     |                     |\<-- Ack (999) \---|                                        |    (msg\_id: 999\)   |  
     |\<-- Sent Ack (999) \--|                 |                                        |\<-- Delivery Ack \---|  
                                             |                                        |    (msg\_id: 999\)   |  
                                             |\<-- Delivery Ack \-----------------------|

> 1. **User A** sends a message frame with a client-side temporary ID over WebSocket.  
> 2. **WS Gateway 1** forwards the payload to the **Message Service**.  
> 3. **Message Service** assigns a globally unique, monotonically increasing message\_id (e.g., Snowflake ID) and writes the message to primary DB.  
> 4. **Message Service** checks **Session Store (Redis)** to locate **User B**’s gateway node (Gateway 2).  
> 5. Message is delivered via Gateway 2 to **User B**.  
> 6. **User B** sends back a Delivered ACK, updating the message state in DB and alerting **User A**.

## **5\. Deep Dive: Typing Indicators & Online Presence**

### **Typing Indicator Problem: Extreme QPS Bottleneck**

If a user types 60 words per minute, every single keystroke sending a server event generates **5 to 10 QPS per user**.  
For ![][image2] concurrent active typing users, naive routing results in **5M to 10M QPS**, which can exhaust infrastructure bandwidth and crash message queues.

#### **Optimization Strategies for Typing Indicators**

> 1. **Client-Side Debouncing / Throttling:**  
   * Client emits typing\_start event *only once* when user begins typing.  
   * Client enforces a timer window (e.g., ![][image13]). Subsequent keystrokes inside this window are suppressed.  
   * Client sends typing\_stop when user stops typing for ![][image14] or hits Send.  
> 2. **No Persistent Disk Storage:**  
   * Typing state is strictly ephemeral. It is never saved to disk databases (Cassandra/Postgres).  
> 3. **In-Memory Pub/Sub Routing:**  
   * Route typing indicators directly through **Redis Pub/Sub** or lightweight WebSocket Gateway routing table directly to active room participants.

Client Types \-\> \[Debounce 3s\] \-\> WS Gateway \-\> Redis Pub/Sub (Channel: chat\_123) \-\> WS Gateway B \-\> Receiver B

### **Online Presence System (Heartbeat Engine)**

Tracking online/offline status requires managing real-time state when clients abruptly disconnect due to lost cell signal, app crashes, or network switching.

#### **The Heartbeat Mechanism**

> 1. **Heartbeat Signal:** Client sends periodic lightweight ping frames over WebSocket every ![][image15].  
> 2. **TTL Key Management in Redis:**  
>    SET presence:user\_123 "online" EX 45

   * If the ping is received, refresh expiration timer to ![][image16].  
   * If the client loses connection abruptly, the Redis TTL naturally expires in 45s, and key expiration triggers an event transitioning status to offline.  
> 3. **Graceful Disconnect:** On explicit application logout or closure, client sends disconnect frame, immediately setting key to offline.

## **6\. Offline Message Delivery & Synchronisation**

When a recipient is offline, messages cannot be pushed directly via WebSockets.

### **Offline Storage & Retry Architecture**

> 1. **Detection:** Message Service checks Redis Session Store and finds no active connection for **User B**.  
> 2. **Persistent Queueing:** Message is saved in Cassandra/DynamoDB with status STORED\_UNREAD.  
> 3. **Push Notification Fallback:** Message Service enqueues a job to APNs (Apple) / FCM (Google) to show a system banner notification.

### **Reconnection Synchronization Protocol**

When User B regains internet connection and reconnects:

> 1. **Handshake & Auth:** Re-establish WebSocket connection to a WS Gateway.  
> 2. **State Verification:** Client sends its last received checkpoint: last\_received\_message\_id \= 10045\.  
> 3. **Catch-up Pull:** WS Gateway requests unread messages from database:  
>    SELECT \* FROM messages\_by\_chat   
>    WHERE chat\_id \= 'chat\_123'   
>    AND message\_id \> 10045   
>    ORDER BY message\_id ASC   
>    LIMIT 100;

> 4. **Batch Delivery & Ack:** Server pushes missing messages in batches. Client updates local database (SQLite/Room/CoreData) and returns a batch ACK.

## **7\. Data Model & Schema Design**

For ultra-high write throughput and horizontal distribution, Wide-Column NoSQL databases (e.g., **Apache Cassandra** or **AWS DynamoDB**) are preferred over traditional SQL.

### **Messages Table (messages\_by\_chat)**

Designed to support fast sequential retrieval of messages in a given chat room.  
CREATE TABLE messages\_by\_chat (  
    chat\_id uuid,  
    message\_id timeuuid, \-- Snowflake or TimeUUID for ordering  
    sender\_id uuid,  
    content text,  
    media\_url text,  
    status text, \-- SENT, DELIVERED, READ  
    created\_at timestamp,  
    PRIMARY KEY (chat\_id, message\_id)  
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message\_id DESC);

> * **Partition Key (chat\_id):** Distributes messages across cluster nodes based on conversation ID.  
> * **Clustering Key (message\_id):** Orders messages chronologically on disk within each partition.

## **8\. Group Chat Scaling (Fan-out Strategies)**

Group chats present unique challenges because a single message must be distributed to ![][image17] members.

### **Small to Medium Groups (![][image18])**

> * **Fan-out on Write:**  
  * When a message is sent to group\_abc, the server fetches all ![][image17] member IDs.  
  * Server writes a single message entry into group history, then publishes ![][image17] event tasks to Kafka.  
  * Worker nodes push the message to each online member's active WebSocket connection.

### **Large Broadcast Channels / Mass Groups (![][image19])**

> * **Fan-out on Read:**  
  * Writing to thousands of individual user delivery queues causes system write spikes.  
  * Instead, post the message **once** to the group channel bucket.  
  * Active online users pull from the shared group feed while connected, avoiding ![][image17] duplicate write operations.

## **9\. Summary Checklist for Interviews**

> 1. **Establish WebSockets:** Explain why WebSockets are mandatory for bi-directional real-time communication vs. Long Polling.  
> 2. **Address Typing Indicator Scale:** Show awareness of QPS amplification. Explain client debouncing and ephemeral Redis Pub/Sub routing without DB persistence.  
> 3. **Explain Heartbeats for Presence:** Describe Redis TTL-based expiration for handling unexpected socket terminations.  
> 4. **Detail Database Partitioning:** Partition messages by chat\_id with message\_id as clustering key in Cassandra/DynamoDB for high write availability.  
> 5. **Clarify Offline Sync:** Use monotonic IDs (message\_id) to allow clients to cleanly request missed logs upon reconnecting.
